narrative:
The model estimated a 62.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain, but it is above the threshold used here, so your law school application was rejected because the predicted risk was considered too high.

The strongest reason was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.40 it is above the average of 3.23 among accepted students, but in your case this was still the top-ranked factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. The second most influential factor was your third-year class rank. You were in the 9th decile, well above the accepted-student average of about 5.79, and this factor pushed toward passing. The third factor was your family income bracket: upper-middle income added some risk toward failure, although this bracket is common among accepted students (45.4%).

Because two of the three leading factors moved the estimate toward failure, the model landed above the rejection threshold despite the positive signal from your third-year rank. Your application was therefore denied on a predicted bar-exam risk, not on gender or race.

You should ask admissions for an individualized review or appeal, explain the context behind your GPA and strong third-year performance, and ask what evidence could rebut the prediction. Consider bar-readiness advising or prep support, and if reapplying, submit updated academic or test information that shows reduced risk.
